column4: The source's dictionary branch for ظ ه ر makes the back a riding beast carrying loads; this ayah explicitly has animals bear heavy loads to a distant town that people could reach only with hardship, joining the caravan's burden and difficult road to a divine mercy.
This ayah names ships and livestock as things people ride, the exact transport scene that lets the source hear the surah's “back” as a mount rather than only a body part.
The source's camel-back reading meets the ayah's “on their backs” (ظُهُورِهَا): riders are to remember their Lord for this provision, so mounting and remembrance form one scene.
The rider's utterance in the source continues in this ayah: “we are returning to our Lord” (لَمُنقَلِبُونَ), making the journey's destination part of the mount's remembrance.
The source's travel-worn camel becomes an explicit pilgrimage mount here: people come on lean camels (ضَامِرٍ) from distant passes, linking bodily wear to a purposeful journey toward worship.
Like the source's ready riding beast, these cattle are made for people to ride and to eat from; this adds the animal's provision to its transport role.
The source makes a camel a means of reaching the road's destination; this ayah says people reach needs they hold in their breasts by riding cattle and are carried on them and ships.
The source's mount is a prepared animal for riding; this ayah names horses, mules, and donkeys made for riding and adornment, extending the caravan's set of mounts.

The source's camels move between pasture and watering/resting places; this ayah describes livestock returning home in the evening and being driven out to pasture in the morning, giving the route a daily rhythm.
The source treats the loaded camel as a mercy of animal travel; this ayah names livestock's warmth, other benefits, and food, filling out the material provision behind that journey.
After the source's distant-camel pilgrimage, this ayah says pilgrims mention God's name over grazing livestock and feed the needy; it supplies the devotional and charitable purpose of the arrival.
The source turns the road toward the Lord into an arrival; this adjacent pilgrimage ayah contributes the rites to be completed and the circumambulation of the Ancient House.
The source's tame, rideable beast is echoed by cattle made submissive (سَخَّرْنَاهَا لَهُمْ), some of which people ride; it makes the animal's fitness for carrying human beings explicit.
This continuation adds milk and other benefits to the subdued animals of 36:72, completing the source's picture of the mount as a providential animal.
The source hears a caravan mount in the surah's back; this ayah explicitly says people are carried on animals and ships, placing the loaded animal beside sea travel.
The source's pack camel bears a load; this ayah divides livestock into “carriers” (حَمُولَةً) and low-to-ground animals, directly naming the load-bearing class.
The source's caravan carries people along a road; this ayah says humanity is carried on land and sea and provided good things, widening the transport image beyond camels.
The source's camels come to a water stop; here each of the twelve groups is given a known drinking place (مَشْرَبَهُمْ), making a settled, allotted water station part of a people's journey.
This repeated account again gives each group its own drinking place (مَشْرَبَهُمْ); it confirms the water-stop scene of 2:60 and adds the setting of Israel's wilderness provision.
The source's camel is watered on the road; Moses reaches a well where shepherds water their flocks and two women hold theirs back (تَذُودَانِ), a concrete human-and-herd water stop.
After watering the flocks, Moses turns to shade and asks his Lord for whatever good He sends; this brings the source's completed task and turning toward the Lord into a single travel-side scene.
The source's camels rest at pasture and come to water; this ayah pairs the earth's water and pasture (مَاءَهَا وَمَرْعَىٰهَا), showing the two necessities of that stop.
The source names pasture as a place for camels to remain; this ayah identifies the pasture and cattle as provision for people and their herds, completing 79:31's water-and-grass scene.
The source's dictionary entry names a camel resting in pasture; this ayah names fruit and fodder (أَبًّا) among what the earth brings forth, and 80:32 says it is provision for people and livestock.
The source explicitly places camels at pasture; this ayah names pasture's yield as enjoyment and provision for people and livestock (لَكُمْ وَلِأَنْعَامِكُمْ).

The source's camel must stop for water before continuing; this food sequence begins with rain poured down (صَبًّا), whose neighboring verses 80:26 and 31–32 show the earth producing pasture for livestock.
This ayah says the earth is split open in the provision sequence that leads to the source's pasture scene; 80:31–32 identify its yield as fodder and provision for cattle.
Grain is the first named crop in this sequence; the source's camel rests at pasture, and 80:31–32 complete how the earth's growth feeds livestock.
Grapes and green growth are another stage in the sequence leading to pasture; 80:31–32 name fodder and its provision for livestock, connecting growth to the source's feeding stop.
Olives and date palms extend the food sequence whose endpoint is pasture for animals in 80:31–32, matching the source's image of a journey sustained by animal fodder.
Dense gardens continue the earth's provision sequence; 80:31–32 complete it with fodder and provision for livestock, the pasture behind the source's camel stop.
The command to consider food opens the sequence that ends with pasture for livestock in 80:31–32, supplying the source's grazing camel with an account of its provision.
The source builds a caravan and a water stop; this ayah has a caravan arrive and send its water-drawer to lower a bucket, joining travel, water, and the discovery of a carried human being.
The source's camel is a useful mount that prompts remembrance of the Lord; here camels are God's signs, lined up for sacrifice while His name is mentioned, a ritual boundary for the same animal.
The source describes camels coming to water; Salih's she-camel has an appointed drinking turn (شِرْبٍ), an explicit counterpart to water being measured for animals.
Where the source's caravan depends on the camel's water stop, Salih commands his people not to harm the she-camel; this makes care for the watering animal a boundary before its slaughter.
The source's camel is preserved as a working mount; here the people hamstring the she-camel after the shared watering arrangement, a stark reversal of animal care.
The source gives the camel a central place in the road image; this passage calls Salih's she-camel a trial and commands watchfulness, turning the animal itself into a sign.
The source's watering stop is measured; this ayah explicitly divides water between the people and the camel by turns, making the camel's drink a public allotment.
The source's caravan needs its camel alive for the road; this continuation says the people called their companion, who hamstrung the camel, reversing the shared watering order of 54:28.
The source's camel reaches a place to drink; Salih points to God's she-camel and says she has her turn at the water, another explicit water-sharing scene.
The source's camel is a useful mount and carrier; the next ayah reports that Salih's people hamstrung the water-sharing camel, the opposite fate for a working animal.
The source gives a camel its place in a journey; Salih's people are shown God's she-camel as a sign, opening another Quranic camel scene.
The source's camel bears people through the road; this continuation says the Thamud hamstrung the she-camel, making destruction of the animal a reversal of the source's useful mount.
The source links a camel with the Lord and the road; Salih identifies God's she-camel and her turn to drink, joining divine claim to the animal and its water.
The source's camel remains a working companion on the road; this next ayah says the people denied the warning and hamstrung her, the opposite outcome.
The source's camel drinks on its route; this passage contrasts that sustaining stop with scalding water for the condemned, setting up the thirsty-camel comparison of 56:55.
The source presents water as a camel's needed provision; this ayah says the condemned drink like thirst-crazed camels, turning that same need into punishment.
The source's camel is tended, loaded, and ridden; this ayah pictures valuable pregnant camels left unattended at the Last Hour, reversing human care for a working beast.
The source's mount rests at pasture; this ayah says God brings forth pasture (الْمَرْعَىٰ) and then makes it dark, dried stubble, adding the grass's passing cycle to the route.
This continuation makes the pasture of 87:4 wither into dark stubble; it sets the source's grazing stop within a cycle of provision that does not last.

The source's caravan follows a road with a place to stop; this ayah places towns between the blessed cities and apportions travel between them (وَقَدَّرْنَا فِيهَا السَّيْرَ), describing measured stages and safe day-and-night movement.

The source's road has a watering place where the caravan remains; this sequel has Saba ask for far-separated journeys (بَاعِدْ بَيْنَ أَسْفَارِنَا), a specific reversal of connected, safely measured stages.
The source's wide-striding horse and broad road need open ground; this ayah says God spread the earth out, while 71:20 completes the purpose as travel along wide paths.
The source names a broad road for a caravan; this ayah explicitly says people may travel through wide paths (سُبُلًا فِجَاجًا), making the route's breadth concrete.
The source's caravan needs a route and stopping landscape; this ayah places firm mountains, rivers, and paths in the earth so people can be guided through it.
This continuation adds landmarks and stars as guides, completing the route-finding scene of 16:15 and giving the source's road a way to be followed.
The source makes the surah a road journey; this ayah says God made paths in the earth so people might be guided, immediately before 43:12–14 names the mounts and their destination.
The source's broad road is a physical route across the earth; this ayah says God made paths there for people to travel, adding a landscape to the caravan image.
The source pairs a camel's road with its pace; this ayah places paths among the earth's mountains so people may be guided, echoing both route and the elevated landscape of 88:19.
The source's journey moves toward the Lord; this ayah tells people to walk the earth's slopes (مَنَاكِبِهَا), seek provision, and remember that resurrection is to Him.
The source's road ends in turning toward the Lord; this ayah promises a wide route and refuge in the earth to one who migrates toward God and His Messenger.
The source says to toil and then turn toward the Lord; this ayah describes a person laboring toward their Lord (كَادِحٌ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ) until meeting Him, making road-work and return explicit.
The source's effort is directed toward its Lord; this ayah says those who strive for God are guided to His paths, joining exertion to divine wayfinding.

The source's caravan has a destination that gives its long walk direction; Moses says he will not stop until reaching the meeting of the two seas, the goal later followed by the travel-fatigue of 18:62.
The source dictionary branch B004 for ن ص ب describes exhaustion from remaining upright; Moses' companion calls their journey's fatigue نَصَبًا, while 18:60 supplies the long journey's goal.
The source's B004 branch of ن ص ب is travel-weariness; this ayah names thirst, fatigue (نَصَب), and hunger endured on God's path as good deeds, giving the loaded road spiritual value.
The source's day-long caravan walk is measured effort; this continuation records every expense and valley crossed by the believers, completing 9:120's account of rewarded travel hardship.
The source dictionary branch B004 of ن ص ب calls bodily weariness nasab; this ayah says no nasab touches the residents of the Garden, making the final resting place a reversal of the road's fatigue.
The source says that when one task is finished, another should begin; this ayah commands leaving trade and hastening to God's remembrance, while 62:10 gives the return to ordinary work.
After the source's “when you are free, then toil,” this ayah sends people back into the land to seek God's bounty and remember Him, completing the work-and-remembrance sequence begun in 62:9.
The source's final turn is toward the Lord with desire; this ayah says the prophets hastened to good deeds and called on God with hope and fear (رَغَبًا وَرَهَبًا), joining effort and longing.
The source describes a whole day's walk and effort; this ayah recognizes people traveling through the land seeking God's bounty and makes the devotional burden responsive to what is easy for them.
The source's effort is a journey toward God; this ayah groups migration, expulsion, harm suffered in God's cause, and a promised Garden, placing travel and hardship within a path of divine reward.

The source sends the traveler onto a demanding road toward God; this ayah rebukes those who “cling heavily to the earth” (ٱثَّاقَلْتُمْ إِلَى ٱلْأَرْضِ) when told to march, explicitly contrasting departure with attachment to the nearer life.

The source camel carries concrete loads on the road; this command to go forth “light or heavy” (خِفَافًا وَثِقَالًا) addresses expeditionaries' conditions, so the load echo is specific but not certainly literal cargo.

The source contrasts the difficult, untrained mount with the easy one; this ayah contrasts an easy gain and short journey with the believers' long, hard expedition, giving the same easy/difficult polarity a travel context.
The source's rider says his mount is prepared for riding; this ayah says the hypocrites would have prepared supplies if they truly intended to set out, reversing readiness for travel.

The source dictionary branch B003 of و ض ع describes an easy pace and its contrast with faster movement; the verse's لَأَوْضَعُوا۟ uses that root for the hypocrites' rapid riding through the ranks, giving the pace word a disruptive social setting.
The source dictionary says “my mount is ready to ride”; this ayah describes people asking the Prophet for mounts, then leaving in tears when none can be found, showing travel depends on provision.
The source's easy and difficult mounts embody opposite routes; this passage begins by naming giving and God-consciousness, with 92:7 completing its consequence as ease made accessible.
This continuation affirms the best reward after giving; 92:7 says such a person is eased toward ease, echoing the source's contrast between a tame, yielding mount and a difficult one.
The source root ي س ر describes an easy-to-follow mount; here God eases (فَسَنُيَسِّرُهُ) the giver toward ease, making the mount's obedient movement a moral path.
The opposite sequence begins with withholding and self-sufficiency; 92:10 completes it by easing that person toward hardship, reversing the source's yielding, easy mount.
This ayah adds denial of the best reward to the withholding sequence; 92:10 completes the consequence as a path made easy toward hardship, the source's difficult route in a moral register.
The source contrasts an untrained, difficult mount with one easy to guide; here the one who withholds is eased toward hardship (لِلْعُسْرَىٰ), making difficulty a path shaped by conduct.

The source uses عُسْر and يُسْر for a hard versus yielding mount; this ayah pairs the same roots in fasting and says God intends ease, not hardship, giving the image a concrete case of religious ease.
The source pairs a hard mount with an easy one; this ayah promises ease after hardship (عُسْرٍ يُسْرًا), adding a temporal passage from difficulty to ease.
The source's yielding mount represents ease; this divine promise says “We will ease you toward ease” (لِلْيُسْرَىٰ), carrying the same root into a promise about the addressed servant's course.

The source dictionary's root ن ق ض pictures journeys as if they dismantled the camel; this ayah warns against a woman who unravels her firmly spun yarn, a direct reversal of held-together work into undoing.

The source uses وَضَعَ for lowering a camel's neck and setting a load down; this ayah says the Messenger removes burdens and shackles (وَيَضَعُ عَنْهُمْ إِصْرَهُمْ وَالْأَغْلَالَ), turning the load image toward relief.

The source's camel bears useful travel cargo; this ayah compares those who do not carry the Torah's responsibility to a donkey carrying books, making weight without understanding the opposite of purposeful transport.

The source's dictionary branches of وَضَعَ include lowering and resting a mount; this ayah says every pregnant woman sets down her burden (تَضَعُ كُلُّ ذَاتِ حَمْلٍ حَمْلَهَا), a bodily reversal of a load carried along a road.
The source explicitly asks the reader to look at the camel; this ayah asks how camels (الْإِبِلِ) were created, making the same animal a sign for reflection.
The source's root ر ف ع names the camel's quicker raised gait; this next question asks how the sky was raised (رُفِعَتْ), extending the look from camel movement to the heavens.
The source's root ن ص ب names exertion and an upright stance; this continuation asks how mountains were erected (نُصِبَتْ), shifting the same posture word to the landscape.
This continuation asks how the earth was spread out, completing the camel-sky-mountain-earth sequence and giving the source's caravan road an opened landscape.

The source's image includes a camel's slow, burdened road and a horse's broad gait; this oath instead opens with chargers panting at speed, an alternate mounted pace whose identification as horses is traditional rather than stated here.
The source's riding animal carries people and loads; this next image has the chargers strike sparks with their hooves, continuing the high-speed mounted scene of 100:1.
The source's caravan travels to reach a destination; these chargers rush at dawn in a raid, giving the contrasting mounted speed a military purpose.
The source's road is a sustained caravan path; this continuation raises dust in the chargers' passage, extending the raid scene begun in 100:1–3.
The source's camel reaches a settled destination; this final line says the chargers penetrate into the midst of a host, completing the contrast with a forceful arrival.
The source contrasts a difficult untrained mount with a tame, readily guided one; this simile shows wild asses (حُمُرٌ مُّسْتَنفِرَةٌ) fleeing from a reminder, an opposite animal response.
This continuation supplies the lion that startles the wild asses in 74:50; the source's trainable riding beast follows a guide, while these animals flee a pursuer.

The source dictionary branch for ن ص ب describes upright exertion; this verse instead uses نُصُبٍ for a set-up marker that crowds rush toward, a distinct lexical branch and a different endpoint from the source's road toward the Lord.

The source's ن ص ب branch describes effort and an upright stance; this ayah's النُّصُب names erected altars where animals are sacrificed, a distinct lexical sense that marks the boundary between a working mount and an animal at a ritual station.
